utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, ma'am. Call the accused are present today. Prosecution it's Mr. McCloskey only. Amongst the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Bourgon, and Mr. Haynes. Good morning to you, Mr. Miljanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. Ms. Fauveau is going to proceed with her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, what was your rank in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a colonel, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was the material situation in the army of the Republika Srpska when you joined it in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can only answer about material and logistics, if that is actually what is being asked of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, indeed that is the question.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Materiel and medical situation in the army of Republika Srpska back in 1993 when I started to familiarise myself with the situation, was disorganised, chaotic, exceedingly complex and I would say entirely disordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you are talking about the chaotic situation, what exactly do you mean by this term "chaotic"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is that the logistics support system was not operating at the required level. The system failed to control the movement of goods and equipment into the army or out of the army. It was impossible to monitor expenditures, and there was no way to reconcile the irreconcilable; namely, the large scale discrepancy between the needs of a war situation on the one hand and the requirements of the men in a situation like that. On the other hand, we had the meager possibilities offered by what was at the time a very modest state, Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... 22 to the witness, please. It's a report on the situation in the Bratunac area dated 23rd of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just, as that's coming up, I'm getting significant feedback in my microphone, if the audio guys could -- it's just between questions, it's very strange, but it's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Could the technicians please do something about it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the Counsel please repeat the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [In English] 5D1022. [Interpretation] Could we show the witness a little bit lower down on the screen, and on English it's the first paragraph on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the paragraph where we can read: "[In English] The logistics support unit of the Bratunac Brigade and other units is increasing critical. There is a fuel shortage and in spite of all the efforts, there is big shortage of all the ammunition and food." [Interpretation] In 1993, were reports of this type usual, customary?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Reports with a similar character were quite usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And what was the situation in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in 1995 changed to some extent, especially in terms of the stability of the functioning of the logistics support system. It was functioning a lot better now, and the procedures took a shorter time to complete. Nevertheless, the supply reserves had already been used up to far greater extent as compared to 1993, and supplies were even more difficult to come by than in 1993. There was nothing really significant in terms of urgency or anything critical, the system was running a little more smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to show you the report of the Drina Corps, the first is 5D1051. This is the report of the 16th of February, 1995. This is on page 2 both in B/C/S and in English, and it's point 6 that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Here we can see that there is a shortage of food, munitions, fuel, and medicines. Were such reports customary in 1995 as well?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. This was a report that was in no way unusual in terms of logistics support.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd now like to show you the report dated 21st of February, in other words, five days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 5D1052. In English it is page 2 point 6 and in B/C/S it's point 6, which is lower down on that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Here again we can see that there is a shortage of certain items, food --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether I should continue because I think that the Prosecutor still has problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I have the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have the same problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently the Defence is suffering from the same problem as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have some background noise, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a slight humming tone, but it's not disturbing me, but anyway, we need to do something about it. Usually, if one turns -- this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no problem going on, it's just annoying and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know it's -- I can imagine, because I've had it in the past. So it's annoying, definitely, but let's proceed, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So five days later, you received another report from the same corps, still talking about the shortage of certain food items. I'd like to know whether the army of the Republika Srpska and its Main Staff were in a position whereby they could solve this problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's leading and somewhat vague. Does she mean by "you" the Main Staff, or has this witness actually reviewed this report? If we could just clear that up, then I won't have a problem. It's just not clear if he's reviewed this report himself or if this is something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I said on page 3, line 23, that it was the report of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My objection is -- well, two, it was leading because she said "he reviewed it," but it's more foundational, does he normally get reports like this from the Drina Corps and review them, and has he reviewed this one himself at the time of the events? I think it has a lot more substance that way if we get a little foundation without ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can repeat what we were talking about yesterday at the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you receive reports from the corps?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Such reports would arrive at the rear command post of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, but not ones like these. Broader, reports, proper logistics reports, I have never received a report like this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As to the contents of this part, dealing with logistical support, in other words this report, does that corps respond to the broader reports that you used to receive at the time from the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, if we look at item 6, it is a summary and a conclusion of the logistics report that the logistics organ of the Drina Corps would submit to their superior who was the assistant commander for logistics of the Main Staff of the army Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we come back to the question that I put to you earlier, I would again like to show you another report which is 5D1062. This is another report from the Drina Corps dated the 5th of April, 1995. In English, we're referring to page 2, and in B/C/S I'd like you to scroll down to point 6, which is the final paragraph in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So in April 1995, the Drina Corps reports on the shortage of certain food items. I'd like to know whether the army of the Republika Srpska was trying to solve such requests from the logistics sector of the Main Staff? I'd like to know whether the logistics unit of the Main Staff of the army Republika Srpska tried to solve these requests, to satisfy these requests, from the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, these requests were always considered. Whenever possible, one took action. If not, they weren't ignored, but they couldn't be dealt with so the situation would continue until such time that it could be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The reports that we've just seen came from the Drina Corps, what was the situation in the other army corps?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, logistics reports from all units of the army Republika Srpska looked very much alike. The substance was the same throughout as we have seen in these three reports that we have just reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who was in charge of supplying materiel goods; in other words, equipment, munitions, food stuffs, fool, who was responsible for the supplies to the army?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the army of Republika Srpska the body in charge was the government of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And how did the government know what the army of the Republika Srpska's needs were?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska would inform the government on its needs in terms of supplies, in terms of weapons and ammunition. Certain requests were forwarded to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And who, from the Main Staff, was in charge of informing the government?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant commander of the Main Staff of the army Republika Srpska for logistics, General Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know how often such requests were sent to the government?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it would be a good idea for me to speculate on this. General Djukic often went to the government. I don't know how often he sent such requests, but based on my knowledge and all of the other organs who took part in preparing such requests, it would be ones at the end of the year in relation to the army's needs for the following year and perhaps another time during the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that General Djukic often went to the government, did you attend any of the government sessions?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Whenever General Djukic was not able to make it there, and issues were discussed that had to do with the army's materiel and medical situation, I would then attend.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could both the witness's microphones be switched on, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know whether General Miletic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you switch on the other microphone as well, please. All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can perhaps you could clarify what you mean by "sessions." Is this Assembly sessions or some meetings or what because that's not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest that you even repeat the whole question, because only part of it appears in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know which question the Prosecutor is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think now looking at it, he is probably referring to the previous one which said -- you said that: "General Djukic often went to the government, did you attend any of the government sessions?" He wants a clarification as to which sessions you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the government is made up of an Assembly, and other than that government and Assembly, I don't know what further clarification I can add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But it's clear now --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I said. I said I was saying that these were government sessions, if I meant Assembly sessions I would have said "Assembly sessions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. It's different. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no idea what government session means, and I don't know if the witness does. And maybe it's a translation, but "sessions" can mean anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I stand with you, here, because to me, for example, government sessions is incomprehensible. I don't know what you would be referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in French, government session is a common term. English is neither my mother tongue nor my second language. I do not know how this should be translated. "Sjednica vlade" means government session; in French, "session du gouvernement." And it is a current term in French. I don't know how better to explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To be fair to my learned friend, that term was commonly used in the Krajisnik case, "government sessions," in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I wasn't in the Krajisnik case, so I still need some kind of explanation what is meant by "government session," whether it's -- yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I loathe to give evidence, but the body led by the prime minister, as I understand it, as opposed to the presidency sessions, they are different, government sessions. So as I said it was the body led by the prime minister which consisted of the various members of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you mean to say prime ministerial cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then I understand it. Cabinet of ministers, basically. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall repeat the question. Cabinet of ministers doesn't mean much in French.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you attend government sessions or sessions of the cabinet of ministers?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours I did attend sessions chaired by the prime minister and in which certain government ministers took part.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether General Miletic attended such sessions of the cabinet of ministers or government sessions?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know that General Miletic attended a government session once.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Aside from supplies from the government, did the army of Republika Srpska have any other source of supply?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the army of Republika Srpska used the reserve left from the former Yugoslav Peoples' Army. Depending on the kind of materiel or equipment it also received help from abroad or from outside from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say that it received help from abroad or from outside the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, what type of help -- or, rather, how did this help reach the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's an important, probably mistranslation. I'm sorry to interrupt, but I'm not -- or it's not what he said. She said: "Did he receive help outs the FRY?" He said he got help from the FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you received help from abroad and from the republic of Yugoslavia. How did this help, this assistance, reach the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am going to answer this question the way I understood it. It was called "assistance," and it arrived in various ways. I can refer to some of them. Various individuals who were called upon or not called upon from municipalities, enterprises both from in the army or from outside of the army in this wartime nightmare, felt called upon to secure something from somewhere. This is one of the questions that actually contributed to the chaos that I mentioned in responding to the question of materiel and health supplies in 1992 and 1993. This kind of "assistance," I put that in quotes, is something that I am well familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In certain situations, could the army of the Republika Srpska purchase certain goods directly, certain materiel goods and equipment?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the time when I came to the army of Republika Srpska, the army did not have a budget and -- or financial means to procure the articles it required in the way that I was aware that the JNA was able to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the army of Republika Srpska obtain any assistance, any materiel assistance, from the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember some situations when the army received assistance from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you 5D843.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And before it arrives, I would like to know whether you could tell us which situation you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information comes from conversations of General Djukic that he had with us at some meetings that -- or the chiefs of services when he addressed them. When we were asked to state our requirements in fuels and for the purposes of compensation for the use of roads and for the service of repairs of those roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether this document is referring to precisely the thing that you have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we enlarge the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this evidently covers the same questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether certain UNPROFOR units obtained supplies in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether they obtained supplies, no, I don't recall that they did. No, or can you please clarify for me? I didn't quite understand. What sort of supplies?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you know the president of the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you 5D1324, because I believe that this will refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you see the start of this document, we can read: "[In English] On August 6th, the president of the Bratunac municipality and Colonel Miljanovic discussed the supplying of the Dutch battalion by companies from Bratunac." [Interpretation] Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was such a talk but I really cannot definitely say that the Mayor of the Bratunac -- or the president of the Bratunac municipality was involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Dutch Brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Dutch Battalion, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: -- received provisions from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, did I read that there was an initiative like that, but I don't know where it came from. And I was informed about it, obviously, at this encounter which was just by coincidence. I don't know how it came about that the president of the Bratunac municipality encountered me. And the interpretation I put here is that -- I mean, it was evidently a logical one because the problem was that the army of Republika Srpska didn't have any right to trade, so the procedure that was previously agreed was not something that was harmonized with the government laws. They were not paying some sort of tax or something, so I pointed this out to the president or the person whoever it was that I spoke to, and that if this regulation is adhered to, then there should be no problems. I think that after that, this was resolved, but I think this is the way it happened as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Was it customary that the Main Staff officers had contacts with the local civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was not forbidden. I mean, quite the contrary, I had contacts of that nature. I don't know how much others maintained such contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Fine. I would like to move on to another subject now. Can you tell us who decided which army corps received a quantity of fuel, who decided on the quantity of fuel that was to be allocated to a given army corps?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the commander of the Main Staff made these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And what was the role of the logistics unit as regards this decision taking?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the commander could ask for the opinion or recommendations of the rear command chief, but then he would act pursuant to his own decision no matter what sort of proposals he heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the logistics unit have a role to play when the commander decided on the quantity to be allocated to individual army corps or units once a decision had been taken?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And who distributed this fuel? So materially, technically, who distributed the fuel to the different corps?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I already said this, but I mean it was the commander who allocated this. But if you allow me, I would like to explain the main procedure, briefly, how this was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you interested in this, Ms. Fauveau, or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there was a -- an interpretation problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When the commander decides that in certain -- that certain corps will obtain a certain amount of fuel, who is responsible for the actual distribution of that fuel to those corps?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fuel that was obtained from somewhere and came to the army of Republika Srpska, and the commander would, let's say, write on a document 1st Krajina corps this much and that corps that much and that corps that much and so on and so forth. Most frequently, he would then write, The rest should be housed at the bases. And that's what would come to the logistics assistant. He would then look at that and he used to be -- I mean, it was General Djukic, he used to take the quantity allocated for the bases, would distribute different quantities that would go to the different bases. And most often the clerk from the technical service was entrusted with fuel distribution, he would receive this list. And then that organ would then be in charge of executing this to the letter. This is the procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that the witness referred to a number of bases where the fuel would be distributed, but it was too fast to be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we have that problem to deal with, and you're objection? Or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a foundational, perhaps, there has been no mention of the bases, and I think that would help clarify some of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And in addition, Mr. Miljanovic, the interpreters had problem catching up with the speed with which you are testifying. You mentioned a number of bases where the fuel would be distributed, different bases. The interpreters believe that they did not translate everything that you said. Let me read out to you what we have in the transcript, and then, perhaps, if there is something missing you can fill it in. You said: "He would then look at that and he used to be -- I mean, it was General Djukic, he used to take the quantity allocated for the bases, would distribute different quantities that would go to different bases. And most often, the clerk from the technical service, was entrusted with fuel distribution. He would receive -- I think most often the clerk from the technical service who was entrusted with fuel distribution would receive this list. And then that organ would then be in charge of executing this to the letter." Is there anything else that you said that I didn't mention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I listen to what I said, it does not reflect absolutely what I expressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then, please, could you clarify and go, again, through this answer and your reply and make us understand better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly, very gladly, Your Honour. When General Djukic received the act of a specific content, whereby he's being informed that for the requirements of the army of Republika Srpska, the government secured a certain quantity of fuel. Then, on the document, the commander of the Main Staff would write in his hand, To the 1st Krajina Corps, this quantity of fuel; the 2nd Krajina Corps, such and such a quantity; the Drina Corps would receive a certain quantity; and so on until he covered all the corps. And then, there would be a remark underneath, The remaining quantity to be distributed in the logistics bases. General Djukic would then add, in his hand, 14th rear base, a specific quantity, the 35th logistics base, also he would note down a quantity, the 27th logistics base, such and such a quantity, the 30th logistics base, such and such a quantity, and then he would initial that. Then he would call, most often, the clerk of the technical service in charge of fuel from the technical sector, the person is -- would be from the technical sector, he would hand over the document to this person and order him to execute it to the letter. That person would then proceed according to the procedure. Your Honours, do I need to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I'm even doubting in my mind whether we need all this detail. I don't know, I don't want to make decisions for you, Ms. Fauveau, but I think too much detail. If you steer the witness to where you want him to go and make him understand that a clean answer, short and sweet, is better. I think we will proceed much faster.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Which base supplied the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps received its supplies from the 27th logistics base of the army of Republika Srpska and the 35th [Realtime transcript read in error, "25th"] logistics base of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 18, line 18, it is the 35th logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did these two bases only supply the Drina Corps or did they provide supplies to other corps?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They also supplied other corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Which corps received supplies from the 35th base?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 35th logistics base supplied the East Bosnia Corps as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the 35th logistics base was located where?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I were to give a short answer, the question would need to be formulated differently. The base command was in Bijeljina. The base had a certain territory, and this is according to the territorial organisation of the army, and on that territory it was -- its duty to supply logistically the units in that territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that answer your question, Ms. Fauveau, or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was interested in knowing about the headquarters of the base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Foundational, these bases, who are they subordinated to? That's the first time they have been discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could you explore that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but the witness spoke about this yesterday. I can go through all of his testimony from yesterday again, but the witness has already answered that question. I can put it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: To whom were these bases subordinated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, but look at the record, that's not correct. There was a brief reference to base, and he never explained what logistics bases were, who they were subordinated to, none of that. It's just not there, unless I was gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time. He's going to answer it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, logistics bases of the army of the Republika Srpska, the 14th, the 35th, the 27th, and the 30th, those were directly subordinated to the assistant commander of the Main Staff of the army Republika Srpska for logistics, General Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As the 35th base provided supplies to the Drina Corps and to the Eastern Bosnia Corps, how did the 35th base know which amount of fuel, stored there, was to go to the Drina Corps and which amount was to go to the Eastern Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer this question in the following way, Your Honours: The fuel reserves of the Drina Corps were kept in warehouses where the reserves of the army of Republika Srpska were kept, too, in the warehouses within the military bases in separate facilities. And when I say "facilities ," I mean buildings; and when I say "warehouses," I mean a building with a number of such facilities. And there was no mingling there, we knew exactly what the corps reserves were and what the reserves were that belonged to a base. That is if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And what was the situation with munitions? The munitions that were stored at the 35th base?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the situation with ammunition, in that regard, was the same. Just to keep me from explaining --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... to show the witness P3820.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you see which unit received the munition indicated on this document, and it's military post 7042, Bratunac. And if we go down to the bottom of the page -- I'll repeat the question. It seems there was no interpretation. So I'm sorry, can we go back up to the top of the page, please. The unit -- that was the receiving unit we see from this document, in other words, that received the munitions indicated on this document, is military post 7042 Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we could now scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Here we can see that these resources went directly from the 35th base. Have you seen this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And on the left-hand side we can see that there was approval given by a certain Basovic, do you know who Basovic is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Major Basovic was a clerk, was someone working with the technical service that was attached to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could the 35th base send these munitions to the Bratunac Brigade with the approval of the officer of the Drina Corps, or did it need a further approval from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this ammunition could have left the warehouse of the 35th logistics base. There is at a storage facility within that warehouse holding the reserves of the Drina Corps. The warehouse, as a building, was the responsibility of the Drina Corps, and that is where its reserves were kept. As for physical control, in terms of a facility such as this one, and this was a specialty facility if I can put it that way, because ordinance was kept there. Now, that was something that was the responsibility of the 35th logistics base. In that same warehouse, there were storage units holding the reserves of the 35th logistics base as well. Now, there was an authorisation from this clerk, Basovic, and whatever left the compound, pursuant to this authorisation, was something that left the Drina Corps; and the Drina Corps was perfectly within its rights. Nevertheless, without approval or authorisation from officers of the 35th logistics base, nothing could leave the unit, or, indeed, enter the unit. And I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau Ivanovic, I think we have seen this document before, but since there is no English translation, could you ask the witness to read the handwritten parts of columns 36, where 35th logistical base appears? No, down, down in there, bottom part.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, could you read what you see after the number "36," the heading, and also the handwritten part.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This equipment went directly from the 35th logistics base," and then there is something that I can't quite read, "Bisic, Tisic D." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you something about the principle of subordination. The officers of the brigade - and I'm referring to the logistics platoon - did they address themselves directly to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot rule out the possibility that officers from the brigades that went directly to the Main Staff. But this would have constituted a violation of the subordination principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you document 5D1009.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know what was the position of the officers of the Main Staff as compared to the officers of the brigade which addressed themselves -- or who addressed themselves directly to the Main Staff? Sorry, there is an error in the interpretation. I'll begin again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in the meantime, let's hear what Mr. McCloskey has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just like the last question, "officers of the logistic bases," that's awfully broad. And "officers of the Main Staff" is awfully broad, I don't see how it can be asked or answered and have it make any sense. Or, it certainly doesn't help us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau, having heard Mr. McCloskey, you were going to refer the question in any case?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [In English] Officers of logistic bases [Interpretation] I don't see where it is "officers of logistics bases," perhaps the Prosecutor can give me the precise reference of the section he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was the question you asked immediately before that, about subordination. And you said -- and he said they couldn't go directly to the Main Staff and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's, at least in mine, it's page 23, the first four lines: "I'd like to ask you something about the principle of subordination. The officers of the brigade," and then we have here, "and I'm referring to the logistics platoon." In other words, you are saying the officers of the logistic platoon, did they address themselves directly to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the suggestion there is the commander of the logistic base can't address himself to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau, let's -- let her handle it and then we will see whether Mr. Miljanovic can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think the witness has answered that question, and what is more I wasn't talking about the bases, I was talking about the brigades. And there is an error in the interpretation. I do not see where the Prosecutor found a reference to the base, but I'll repeat it anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are wasting time. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I entirely agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, does this document confirm what you said; in other words, when an officer of the brigade addressed himself directly to the Main Staff, that was tantamount to a violation of the principle of subordination?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let's now refer to a slightly different situation. When an officer of the logistics department of the corps was to address himself to the Main Staff, to whom would he address himself?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as communication within the army of Republika Srpska was concerned, it was a perfectly legitimate thing, and normal, should I say, for the assistant commander of the corps for logistics to address directly the assistant commander for logistics for the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. Likewise, the chief of the technical service within the command, the rear organ of the corps command, would communicate directly with the chief of technical service, his counter-part in the Main Staff of the army Republika Srpska. Some clerks who worked in such commands, for example, a clerk that was in charge of keeping track of ammunition, they would then get in touch with their own counter-parts in a superior command and thus they worked their way up the chain of command in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not receiving interpretation, and I don't know if interpretation in B/C/S is forthcoming either. So I see some of your colleagues indicating that there was no B/C/S interpretation, interpretation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One of the microphones in the booth is not working, hence the absence of interpretation. She's now changed microphones, so it should be working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you so much for your help. There was a technical problem which I understand has now been fixed. So if you could be kind enough to repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who was in charge of logistical support for combat during a military operation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, whenever there was a military operation, logistics support was something that would be organised by whichever unit happened to be organising the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D361. It is a directive from the Main Staff, Directive Number 7.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Have you heard of that directive?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you in particular page 7 in B/C/S and page 8 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at item 6.6, sir.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read item 6.6.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to your experience and according to your knowledge of the Main Staff, who within the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska could have written what is in item 6.6?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure I understand the question. What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, you said you weren't familiar with this directive, but on the basis of your experience of the work carried out within the Main Staff, who, within that Main Staff, could have been in a position to write this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on my experience, on my work with the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, and based, of course, on my training and military education, an item like this could have been proposed to the commander by the assistant commander for logistics alone. Opposed [as interpreted] I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't need this document anymore, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The logistic department of the Main Staff, did it have a role to play in logistic supports for the activities that were planned within subordinate units? [In English] For the combat activities.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the interpretation that I am getting is whether the logistics department of the Main Staff have a role. Whenever there is something that I don't understand, I have no choice but to ask. What is the logistics department that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did the logistics sector of the Main Staff have a role in logistics support of combat activities that were planned within subordinate units within the corps or within the brigades, that is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, any operations planned by subordinate units in terms of logistics were planned and implemented by the logistics organs of those very units. Now, as for the logistics sector of the Main Staff of the army Republika Srpska, they did not plan the corps's operations, or, indeed, the lower level activities by any of the brigades; nor, indeed, were they directly involved in any of these.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the logistics sector of the Main Staff take part in the plan and preparation of military actions around Srebrenica and Zepa during the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, not that I know of. I personally certainly was not involved in anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When did you hear that the army of Republika Srpska had entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not have clear knowledge about that. Nevertheless, I am trying to think back. I seem to remember this was something that I learned from the public media. There was a TV set in the operations room that was always on and people were watching.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us when that was? Could you be more specific as to the date? Or was it the day after, two days after the very day that the army entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would be hard put to pinpoint a date. I remember that it was the same day that it actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember any particular request from the Drina Corps to the logistics sector after the army of Republika Srpska entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't remember a request like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember any particular order given to the logistics sector?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I remember no such order being given to the logistics sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you have some knowledge about buses that went to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you know about those buses?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember when General Djukic spoke to one of the officers from the transport service, and this was in my presence. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he spoke to this officer telling him to prepare a total of 50 buses to be dispatched to Potocari the next day and to report directly to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know where General Mladic [as interpreted] obtained that information?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: General Djukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know if those buses were sent to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have later information indicating that yes, indeed, those buses had arrived in Srebrenica. But I hadn't actually learned about that on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: To be more specific, can you tell us whom those buses belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Buses belonged to the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What unit in particular?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly which unit each of the buses belonged to, but the traffic and transportation officer probably knew exactly what the breakdown was in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, how much more time do you think you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around about 20 minutes, Your Honour. Just before continuing, I would like to correct the -- the record, which is page 27, line 6, rather than saying "opposed," [In English] it should be "proposed, I said."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, after the army of Republika Srpska entered Srebrenica, was the logistics sector of the Main Staff, as far as you know, in receipt of any request for fuel?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no information about the entry of the army of Republika Srpska into Srebrenica or of any requests for fuel. Except for what I had heard on television, is that what you meant? All right. We didn't understand each other, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last sentence of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If the subordinate units, and particularly the Drina Corps, had received such a request, to whom should such a request for fuel have been addressed?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a mistake in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the subordinate units, inter alia the Drina Corps, had made such a request, to whom should such a request have been made?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The fall of Srebrenica is a very unique situation, and if this person is telling us he has no knowledge of it, then it's really not relevant what might happen in a general situation because it doesn't get us anywhere. I mean, if she wants to ask in a general situation who would it go to, I don't mind; but the suggestion that this is something going on in Srebrenica for a person that says he knows nothing about it is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then, Mr. Miljanovic, could you answer it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the usual procedure for communications in that sense is the way that I explained before, and that is if the logistics sector needed to ask for fuel, they would refer to someone at their level; but if the request was made by a commander it would be made to a commander. This is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... P1190. In the English version it's 1190 C and in B/C/S its 1190 B. This is my mistake, 1199. You can't see this on the document, but the date of the conversation is the 16th of July, 1995; and it was at 1912, between Basevic and an unknown individual concerning fuel.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have already told us in reference to another document, who was Basevic and I would like to know whether the Basevic in this conversation is the same person?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's possible, but I cannot state that decidedly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you see in this conversation that there was a certain Miletic who was referred to? Could you tell us whether this might be General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. I don't see here where Miletic is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It's in the first paragraph at the start, the first paragraph of the conversation at 1912.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you read that first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to do that, yes: "The petrol has gone ..." This word is illegible to me, "... I said to Vuletic or Miletic today," I cannot see exactly what it is, "Tetic, when I spoke with him about these requests that -- that Zvornik sent and Sekovici, Zvornik is solved." Is that what I was supposed to read? Your Honours, I cannot conclude from this that it -- it's General Miletic that is being referred to here. If I am supposed to speculate, I mean, I can; but this is an assumption. If it's correct that Basevic is calling and if that is the clerk of the technical service at the Drina Corps command, and if he in the conversation mentions that he spoke with General Miletic, then that in line with what I have already said does not make sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this paragraph, do you see the word "general" anywhere?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I didn't say that. I said if this was the case, but I don't see that it is written anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd now like to show you 1111. In English it is 1111 A, and in B/C/S 1111 B.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Here, as you can see, the conversation was dated 12th of July, 1995, and what I am interested in is in B/C/S at 1220, the conversation at 1220, where two unknown individuals are talking. Just before that, sir, could you tell me whether the General Miletic had a nickname?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, sorry to interrupt you, but I am informed that this document is confidential.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Perhaps this document should indeed not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell me whether General Miletic had a nickname?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall a nickname other than people close to him, when I would be close to him, would refer to him as Mico, his closest associates; but I never referred to him in that way when communicating with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does this conversation tell you that the Miletic mentioned in this could be General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I cannot conclude that from this conversation, that it is, indeed, General Miletic that is being referred to here. It says clearly "Miletic" but as for the rest ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you read this conversation, what conclusion do you draw, that Miletic knew something about the fuel, this Miletic in question, or that he knew nothing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we show the bottom part of the B/C/S to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it is indeed leading, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What conclusion do you draw from reading this conversation as to the Miletic in question and his knowledge about any fuel?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, whether this is suggested or not I read here that the person marked "Y" says he doesn't know either. That personally -- that previously said, "I don't know, I told Miletic." So it can be concluded that this Miletic that's being referred to here doesn't know anything about the fuel.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on to the final subject in my examination. Did you have knowledge about the combat in the Zepa region in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honours, I had -- have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection linked to Zepa and July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do have a recollection of a call from General Mladic. I don't remember the date. When he asked me where General Djukic was; of course, I answered that I didn't know. General Mladic continued the conversation and told me, Tell Djukic to send 50 buses tomorrow to the village of Sjeversko. I cannot recall at what time; and he stopped there and then continued, Well, tell him to call me when you find him. And that's where the conversation ended. I remember that conversation well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And did you convey the message to General Djukic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. As soon as I met General Djukic I informed him about the content of the conversation and General Mladic's order that General Djukic is to call him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know what happened afterwards with these buses?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a certain amount of time, General Djukic called me on the telephone and dictated what I was supposed to write down as an order and send to certain places.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show the witness Exhibit 5D1113.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, you said that General Djukic called you. Do you know where General Djukic was when he called you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, could you take a look at this order.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down to the bottom to show the bottom page to the witness. It's the bottom of the first page in B/C/S and it's page 3 in English. Can we show what is at the bottom left of the page to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We can't actually see the name, but we can read "deputy assistant command for." Do you know who might have signed this order? Do you know who signed the order?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could have signed it, or it could have been signed by someone ordered to sign it by General Djukic in my absence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the part where it says "deputy assistant commander for." There, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recall having written this order?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember the contents very well, but I don't know now whether I actually wrote the order or if I just drafted a brief outline. I am not ruling out the possibility that I did sign it. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness point 1 on this order. And in English it's at the bottom of the page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So we see that it's to do with a bus to transport the ill and the injured, and 50 buses to transport women and children from the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then if you take a look at point 2, page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you explain why this sanitary unit was sent, was dispatched?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see what is written there and I do recall that one bus, as it says here, was sent at 10.00, and that the medic team was sent there in order to take care of the sick and the wounded and to provide first aid in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And now I'd like you to take a look at paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who is Colonel Jovanovic, Milisav?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Milisav Jovanovic is a Colonel, and he's chief of the quarter master section of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to this order, the colonel, through the chief of the operations and training administration, had to provide a military unit, a police unit.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know why this order was given to Colonel Milisav Jovanovic to secure a police unit in the case of need?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can make an assumption with a great degree of certainty why this is written as it is. I remember the tone when General Djukic talked about this previous experience from Srebrenica made him formulate and regulate the pulling out of war booty in this way, from Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What did you hear General Djukic say as regards Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I heard before, sometime after the fall of Srebrenica, he also called me from somewhere, and dictated an order of similar content as this one. But it was about extracting the war booty and a team that had to be sent to Srebrenica to do that. This is what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And was that actually done in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember that the person who was sent to Srebrenica, lieutenant-Colonel or Colonel Strahinja Jankovic, I cannot remember which rank, from the 27th rear logistics base, was entrusted with the execution of this assignment. After a day or two or three, I cannot remember, he sent a report informing that he was not in a position to execute the assignment because he was prevented in doing this by the civilian authority organs, and he referred to, in this context, a certain gentleman with the last name of Deronjic. And after I learned this, I informed General Djukic about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of Colonel Jovanovic who reported what happened at Srebrenica so as to avoid there being any confusion with Milisav Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said Strahinja Jankovic, not Jovanovic if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you said, but it's not in the record, which logistics base was the colonel from?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strahinja Jankovic was from the 27th logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, let's come back to this order. Colonel Jovanovic, if necessary, was to secure a police unit through the chief of the operations and training administration. As regards to the chief of operations and training administration, was he compelled to follow that order?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that Colonel Jovanovic had the obligation to refer to chief of operations and training administration, that was his duty. I don't know how the other person was supposed to act.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We also see this paragraph 5 in this order, where we can read: "[In English] The Drina Corps's command shall order unit command in the Zepa sector to provide all necessary assistance to the team charged with pulling out war booty."

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it states. That is what is written.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the deputy commander for logistics entitled to give orders to the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not entitled to give orders, as you asked. I responded to this question yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is there an explanation for this paragraph 5?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we go back to the beginning of this document, this telegram, is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the top of this page in the English version and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Page 1 in the English version, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There, if you look in the upper left corn, second section, it reads: "Deliver to the 27th POB command, Drina Corps command - PKPO," which means assistant commander for logistics. And just underneath to the attention of GS VRS-KM, which means Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, command post. Therefore, General Djukic dictated the substance of this document to someone and was trying to emphasize that the person he was addressing was the assistant commander for logistics at the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the assistant commander for logistics of the Drina Corps, should he have informed his commander of this order, the commander of Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are questions from the area of command. I am no expert in command, therefore what I have I say is probably irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness P3015. Just before this, the order is dated 19th of July, 1995. The one that we see on the screen. Could we have Exhibit P3015, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You see, sir, that the date of this document is 20th July, 1995. I'd ask for you to read through it carefully.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is there any link between this document and the order dated 19th of July that you saw previously?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may speculate, I can't really say that the assistant commander for logistics of the Drina Corps can familiarise the commander with this, although he had received the other order. If he had received the other ordering then there might well have been a link between the two; or, rather, if the corps commander had been informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether the military police unit ever went to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no information on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When General Djukic dictated to you the order that we saw previously, he said that 50 buses had to be sent to transport the population. Were you surprised by that request?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, surprise can mean a lot of things. In wartime, I tended not to be surprised by anything. I am not sure what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Had there ever been a similar situation before that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember perhaps two situations like that before this one, similar in nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened in those previous situations?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I'm getting the order right --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the first situation would be a situation in which following the clashes between the Croats and Muslim forces in the Travnik and Vitez sectors, there was a mass exodus from that area by the Croats. The Croats then moved to the Serb side in the Vlasic sector. I remember that on that occasion, we organised for the transport. There was the Vares area in Central Bosnia, that's where some people went, and the others went west towards the Republic of Croatia. The other situation that I had in mind occurred again after clashes between the Muslims and the Croats in the Vares sector. Again, the Croats started leaving en mass and crossing to the Serb side. Thousands of people, if I remember correctly. I know that again transportation was provided, I'm not sure what it was off to, and I know that medical teams were dispatched as well as bread and other kinds of aid to support those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, before this testifying yesterday and today, have you had an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was interviewed by the OTP's investigators on the 30th of September and on the 1st of October, 2004, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were preparing for your testimony here, and there was a translation made of some of the parts of that interview, what was your reaction to what had been transcribed from that interview?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd hardly ever had a chance to see how my words were translated. I must say this was a surprise to me. Even now, I can't help admitting when read back the translation of my words hardly ever meet my expectations in terms of what I think I'd said. So that would be the first remark that I would like to place on the record. Secondly, I skimmed the Serbian translation of the interview. My impression at the time was that we had to, to some extent, been talking at cross-purposes despite my best efforts to clarify a number of issues. So that is the essence of what I wished to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Counsel please be asked to speak up and move closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will be asking you several questions in relation to your evidence so far. I will switch places with my colleague since the interpreters seem to be having difficulty hearing me. Mr. Miljanovic, I'm sorry for this brief interruption.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked by the Miletic Defence some questions, and you said that between late March and early June 1995, General Djukic was ill and could not perform his duties. Do you remember saying that, sir? That is at page 28887, yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I remember saying that, but I -- I believe I said until mid-June. Not early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Miljanovic. That was how I understood your answer yesterday. But that's not what the transcript reflected.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much very setting the record straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, you spoke about situations that occurred occasionally when General Djukic was away for a short time. And then you would stand in for him in performing certain tasks at the rear command post. This is a different situation from him being off sick, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, I believe we can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand your evidence correctly, if there was a document for you to sign during the General's physical absence, you would put the word "for" just above the signature, wouldn't you? And that's how the document was dispatched, wasn't it? Whereas when he was permanently away, you would put words like "representing" or "standing in for" or something to that effect. Please correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I believe there has been a misunderstanding. I never said that I put the word "for" over General Djukic's signature and then went on to sign the document. I didn't say that, and I don't remember, as a matter of fact, ever doing that. If you would like me to repeat exactly what it was that I said, I would be all too happy to do that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So we have two situations and in both you would use your own name in the signature line, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you were interviewed by the OTP in September 2004, the OTP asked you a question about meetings, the meetings of the Main Staff commander with his assistants; and this was about the period during which you stood in for General Djukic. I looked at the transcript, and I fully agree with you that the transcript itself is a poor reflection and the English transcript is not very good. That is why I am knot now going back to your subject. As far as I understood by looking at your interview, you said at the time that during the period you were standing in for General Djukic, except for issues such as promoting officers on St. Vitus's day, you never had any meetings of the Main Staff with any of the assistants, none at least that you attended. Do you remember saying that in the interview?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the interview says. I would like to add this, however, there weren't any promotion meetings for St. Vitus's day, but there was a whole day that we referred to as army day. But before both these days there were other personnel board meetings at which proposals were reviewed by subordinate units in terms of promotions, promoting soldiers to a higher rank and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
