utterances.text: With the exception of these two meetings, during the period that you were standing in for General Djukic between late March and mid-June, as far as you knew there were no other meetings at which the commander met his assistants, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly can't think of a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You continue to answer the OTP's questions in that interview. You go on to state that given the fact that Mladic was not your run-of-the-mill officer, he was not really in the habit of holding meetings because he was well aware of the situation throughout the army as a whole. And this, you claimed, was the way he led the army. Do you remember saying that? If not I'd be happy to bring up the relevant paragraph from your interview for your benefit, sir.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember the gist of what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor goes on to ask you, specifically, at page 5 -- 5 out of 9 in the second section, because the interview has several sections so this is probably section 2. The Prosecutor wants to know about the relation between General Mladic and other members of the Main Staff. You answer: "[In English] So in my opinion General Mladic is not a conventional officer. He's not, you know, in stereotypes, so I am not sure whether anyone knew about his decision besides this General Milovanovic, who was his closest associate." [Interpretation] Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor pressed on with his questions about other members of the Main Staff asking you whether they complied with his orders and what their relationship with him was. And then you brought up the example of General Djukic who stood up to Mladic on several occasions. You went on to describe one particular such occasion. You remember saying that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit 6D315.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanovic, I do not believe that you have had a chance to see this document. You know that at some point during late January or early February, 1996, General Djukic was, as a matter of fact, arrested?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, one moment, before you answer the question. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour, as regards the use of this document in this manner. This is a statement made by another individual. If my colleague wants the witness to comment on what General Djukic has said, then he has to put forward the point that he wants to be confirmed or otherwise without actually showing him this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no objection. We've been doing this kind of thing for two years, and I don't see why -- I think it would be unfair at this point to stop it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, do you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the statement is on our 92 quater list. This will be an exhibit. We referred to this in our Defence brief. It's on the list. I see no reason for this statement not to be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Particularly as there has been a motion under 92 quater list, under Rule 92 quater, on the part of my colleague, my colleague should have submitted this request. And, in fact, it was not submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, my apologies to you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've not intention of tendering this exhibit or this document through this witness. I will do that in compliance with the rules, but now I am using my opportunity to talk to the deputy of the person who gave this statement to see if he can make any comments and tell us what, if anything, he knows about certain allegation in the statement. That is the purpose of my using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This statement was made to whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement was made to the BH authorities, the Croat and Muslim federation back when General Djukic was arrested back in 1996, after which he was transferred to The Hague. This is an EDS statement, this is actually an OTP document. As far as I know it was admitted in the Perisic case at the OTP's behest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we have no -- we see absolutely no problem with you, Mr. Krgovic, making use of this part of the -- of Mr. Djukic's statement, interview. The understanding is, as we have always made it clear in the past, that it's what the witness here will testify that will be such in evidence and not the contents of the part of Djukic's statement that you will be reading, okay? In other words, you are not introducing a statement by Mr. Djukic through the use that you are making of this document with this witness. All right? Okay. Let's proceed. I don't know if you wish to repeat the question, or whether you still have it in your mind, in your memory. Mr. Miljanovic, do you wish us to read it out, again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. I didn't understand the question the first time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I asked one, as a matter of fact, in relation to this statement. I was merely asking the witness whether he was aware of the fact that General Djukic had been arrested sometime late in January or early in February 1996 by the BH police, possibly the BH army. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanovic, tell me, he was interviewed by the authorities, he provided a number of statements to the BH authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 5 displayed, that's the B/C/S reference. In the English, it's page 3. I am interested in this part that we are going to read now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Counsel let us know where he's read from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the interpreters would like to know where you are reading from. It will make their life much easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S it's page 5, fifth line from the top. In English, this is on page 3, in the middle of the page begins with Mladic. I'm going to read that: "Mladic -- this meant that despite objections to the way in which the Main Staff worked, some members of the Main Staff expressed their disagreement, and I know that this disagreement was expressed by Gvero, Maric, Salapura, and Djukic. That could be the reason why meetings were not held often and why Mladic did not like negative information."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Have you read this part?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need this document anymore, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanovic, in essence what Mr. Djukic says, does that reflect what you spoke about in your interview more or less?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I'm afraid the transcript did not reflect what you actually read out. If you could read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Miljanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that we do not see the document on e-court anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that could be a problem. Could we have the document back on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 3 in the English and page 5 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read this again, Mr. Miljanovic: "This meant that despite objections to the way in which the Main Staff worked, some members of the Main Staff expressed their disagreement. And I know that this disagreement was expressed by Gvero, Maric, Salapura, Djukic. That could be the reason why meetings were not held often and why -- and also why -- and also that Mladic did not like negative information." Mr. Djukic [sic], I am going to put my question to you again. The people that are referred to here by their last names, General Milan Gvero, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you addressed me as Mr. Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was a slip of the tongue. Mr. Miljanovic, these people that are mentioned here are General Gvero, General Jovo Maric, Colonel Petar Salapura, and General Djukic. Do you agree that these people are referred to here?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have many reasons to believe that they are the persons in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they were all members of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware or, rather, this statement by General Djukic, does that more or less reflect what you also talked about in your interview, or do you have your own opinions or information about that matter?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just to know whether my colleague is going to provide that information, precisely which period was referred to by General Djukic in this -- in this statement, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Djukic was speaking how the Main Staff operated generally and relations within it. It was a question -- I mean, that's how I understood what he said, what the relations were within the Main Staff. He didn't mention a specific time-period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. Mr. Miljanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the late General Djukic had his own way of expressing himself, and he was in that sense a much more skillful man than I am. And probably I would not be able to depict relations in the Main Staff like that, and also the personality of General Mladic himself. But in essence you could say that this does, more or less, reflect what I also wanted to investigators of The Hague Tribunal, but I was not as skillful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for this answer. I will not be needing this document anymore. Mr. Miljanovic, I just wanted to clarify one thing from your testimony yesterday, when you were talking about which organs were located in Han Pijesak and when you were talking about the periods, you were speaking about the military courts and the military prosecutor's office. Do you agree with me that in one period in 1994 the military court and the military prosecutor's office were transferred to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know when that was exactly, but in a period of time they -- excuse me, were transferred from Han Pijesak to the Zvornik sector. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you said then, that's how the question was put, which organs of the Main Staff, as far as I am concerned -- as far as I know the military court and the military prosecutors' office were not part of the Main Staff. They were independent organs, and the administration of these organs was entrusted to the Minister of Defence. I can show you regulations if that will help, but I think that is not something that is controversial in this case.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's very possible that because of my inexperience as a witness I would say something like that which could mean correct. I didn't have full information about whether the ministry or the supreme military court and the Prosecutor's office were part of the Defence ministry or of the Main Staff. I believe that they were in the Main Staff, that's why I answered in that way, but I am not stating that decisively, because I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at of 6D234, please. Can we show that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the break will not be at 12.30 but in four minutes' time. I'm letting you know this so that you regulate yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miljanovic, this is the Law on Military Courts. Can we look at Article 9 of this law, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 2. And that's the page that begins on page 1 in the English version and ends on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanovic, I am going to draw your attention to this paragraph, formation and territorial jurisdiction of the military courts as established by the president of the republic upon proposal of the Ministry of Defence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not see the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I am going to show you some articles and then I will put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Article 27. In English this is on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In Article 27 it says: "Military court judges and judge-jurors shall be appointed or dismissed by the president of the republic. Candidates for the post of military court judges and judge-jurors shall be proposed by the Ministry of Defence upon receiving recommendations from the supreme military court president and the military court to which they will be appointed." And, finally, Article 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "Within the scope of court administration, the Ministry of Defence provides those services which pertain to organisation, personnel, assets, and finances, on which the work of military courts depends." Can we look at the page on B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your question, please, so that we have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanovic, it can be concluded on the basis of this document that military courts have nothing to do with the Main Staff, do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is evident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are continuing the sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, the absence of Judge Kwon. So Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I am not going to show you any other document. We have a document from the Prosecution, so the content is the same. So you will agree me that, as you've already said, since this is not in your jurisdiction you were not informed about the powers of courts and the prosecutor's offices and where they belonged when you were answering that question, which organs of the Main Staff were located at Han Pijesak, do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you are absolutely right. I understood that as which organs were located there, so I hope that I did not commit a major sin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanovic, you confirmed that from the end of March until the middle of June, General Djukic was absent. In that period did you receive any orders or instructions to prepare any orders or directives? You already answered the question that you were not familiar with Directive 7.1. So I'm just asking you about that answer of yours.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall any requests relating to any directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And General Djukic did not tell you or issue instructions for you to prepare any proposals in connection with that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall that either. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. And good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Miljanovic. I want to just first --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon -- I'm sorry. I'm not a general, I never was one, and I'm not one now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go back to while we were on that to 6D315, it's that interview -- or, more likely, an interrogation of General Djukic. I believe it was in 1995, though I think it was after he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There is -- I seem to recall a story where the signs were change and General Djukic's group went to the wrong area and drove right into the hands of the enemy, and he got arrested, correct? That was after the war, I believe.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the signing of the Dayton Accords as the end of war, you are absolutely right because this happened after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You remember that story about him taking a wrong turn or something and him getting arrested?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that story, but I wasn't -- I was absent then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he was subsequently indicted by The Hague Tribunal and transported to The Hague where he died, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he was on provisional release when he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He died after his arrest by The Hague --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I haven't actually answered yet, I'm waiting for this thing to finish. What I know for sure is that General Djukic was returned to Belgrade alive and that's where he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of cancer --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- which he had for a long time. Sorry, we were overlapping and that's my fault. So General Djukic died of cancer that he'd had for a long time, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't confirm that. I know from stories that that's how it was. Well, if it was really that is something that the medical staff, doctors, would know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- going back to that section, I'm told it was -- page 3 in the English and page a 5 in the B/C/S. And I'm going to read a bit more of that than the Counsel did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could start reading the paragraph that starts with: "The Main Staff did not used to meet often ..." You should be able to see that on that page. I'm sorry, I don't have a B/C/S hard copy for you: "It will Main Staff did not used to meet often. The meets were generally used for briefings on the situation, and at some meetings when circumstances arose, ideas were put forward about subsequent tasks about the army of Republika Srpska. A decision would be made beforehand by two, three, or possibly four senior officers. The General concept would be presented --"

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I cannot follow this. Your Honours, I haven't still managed to find the beginning. Something is not quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it must have been on the previous page, Your Honours. It's all right. Now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Problem solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry the -- it's the same place as last time, just a little bit higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "A decision would be made beforehand by two, three, or possibly four senior officers. The general concept would be presented and operatives would be given the task of formulating it. Apart from Mladic, the following would take part in decision-making process: General Milovanovic, General Tolimir, and possibly General Miletic." You were standing in for General Djukic for many months in 1995, do you agree with General Djukic's statement on this page that I just read?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what General Djukic said in this sense is something that I cannot really say much about, other that that's what he said. I didn't attend any meetings where such decisions were adopted in order to be able to say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it goes on and says: "A decision was always based on General Mladic's plan. Mladic was not inclined to listen to other views and particularly not if these did not come from the department that he would deal with the matter. Mladic was inclined to favour his close acquaintances from the past and fellow countrymen regardless of their position." Now, can we say that you surely know, sir, that the General Gvero was a person that Mladic knew in his past. They were JNA officers together and they knew each other from the past, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour. There is no basis for this question, because in this case nobody said that General Gvero or Mladic had known each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What is the reference of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't need a reference to make such an obvious truth, first of all. And it was a nice signal to the witness to say that, and it was completely inappropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Mr. Miljanovic, can you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no knowledge about when General Mladic and General Gvero met for the first time and how long they knew each other. I know when I met General Mladic first and I recall the first time that I met General Gvero:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In this, did you experience -- did you know that General Gvero actually had the ability and courage to disagree with General Mladic as mentioned in this -- this statement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And General Mladic would -- retained General Gvero all throughout the war, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go back a little bit. The time that you were actually standing in for General Djukic, you took over his job during that several month period, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. During that period of two and a half months or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when -- it's been made a little unclear to me, when did you actually cease being standing in for General Djukic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ceased to do that the day he returned to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska having undergone surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What month?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in mid-June 1995, June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you sure it wasn't first part of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am nearly sure. I do allow for the possibility that I might be wrong. I don't know the exact date, but roughly speaking it could have been mid-June. I am quite convinced that it was mid-June, but I can't entirely rule out the possibility that it was early July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, and I think you've told the -- of the investigators before you got -- you got paid more money when you had that bigger job, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't remember telling the investigators. I think I said that yesterday while testifying before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But you did get paid more money. Well, let me show you something and see if it may refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 3950. And it should come up on the list that, if Counsel don't mind, I can just hand him a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, as you can see that this is a document from the Main Staff of the VRS. It's for the personnel -- from the personnel unit in the name of General Skrbic, who we know is the head of that unit. And it's to the Main Staff of the Yugoslav army, the personnel administrator of the 30th personnel centre. And as we can see, we see what this says, that General Djukic has come back from sick leave and resumed his formation duty on the 7th of July 1995. Now, you're aware that you and other career former JNA officers were being paid by Serbian funds out of the 30th personnel centre of the VJ, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really didn't know. And, as a matter of fact, I still don't know what funds were used to pay for the officers' salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you knew you were being paid by Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, this Court has heard repeatedly from career JNA officers. They have all -- well, not all of them, testified on this point. But I never met one that did not know who he was getting his money from. It's particularly difficult because the reserve guys, the reserve officers who were not part of that club, were getting paid by the RS and many times not getting paid. So it's something everyone knew. Take a few seconds, think about your answer. Did you know that you were being paid from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really can't confirm that. I can't say that I knew I was receiving my salary from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you think you were getting your money from, your salary?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was convinced that the issue had been agreed in one way or another who was paying the actual money. That was something I didn't know. One thing is true, I received my salary the same way as before, but I had no idea about the exact source.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not talking about the exact source. I'm saying which country did it come from, Serbia or the RS?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know whether it was from Serbia or from the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did the VRS get most of its ammunition for the war, internal sources or from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have reliable information on this issue, not the kind that would enable me to tell the truth to this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What information do you have on this? Where do you believe the -- most of the ammunition for the VRS came from?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information indicates that the late General Djukic was the person who knew the most about this, and he kept it to himself. I did not venture into that area myself. I did not pry into his business. I did not try to find out where he was getting certain things from or, indeed, what the amounts were arriving from the government of Republika Srpska or the respective amounts that were come from the Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So ammunition did come from the FRY?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that it didn't. I simply can't base a judgment like that or anything. I would rather assume that it did, in fact, come from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You've told us that you knew something about the transportation after the fall of Srebrenica. You learned about the need for buses from General Djukic. What was that for? What were the buses for?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I found out about that, I had no idea what the buses were for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Didn't you take part in drafting the orders and communications to help your boss get those buses?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know what order you are talking about, and I most certainly was not involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you find out what those buses were to be used for? How soon after you heard about it out of Djukic's mouth?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could have drawn an inference, and that's what I assume happened several days later following the next dictate by General Djukic for that team that I spoke about to be dispatched to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you've told us that Djukic said 50 buses needed to go to Bratunac or Potocari the next day, and now you're tell us that several days after that you learned what those buses were for, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't know what exactly the buses were used for, but based on the invitation that we received they said that they needed to evacuate some equipment from Srebrenica by the same buses that had been used to transport civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly but three, four -- possibly five days following the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was there mention of trucks?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Djukic was talking to me about trucks, not about buses, trucks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it's been interpreted as buses until I just asked you about trucks. So did you -- what were those trucks supposed to be used for?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those trucks -- not all of them, they were meant to be used for ferrying some goods or equipment over from Srebrenica. This was supposed to be dismounted [as interpreted] and stored in RS army warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this was some kind of war booty I take it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you might put it that way or at least that's how it was treated at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In the previous answer, it should have been dismantled or taken part, not dismounted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have seen an order with your name on it to that effect by the Defence prior to testifying, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not so, Your Honours. I actually remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, you knew -- so you were involved in issues of war booty for the -- after the Srebrenica campaign and we know from what your answers were about Zepa and the war booty issues of that document. We've seen that you were involved in war booty issues for Zepa as well. So were you the war booty guy at the logistics sector?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I was not the war booty guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we see in a General Djukic was out for a long time from March until July 7th. Does that refresh your recollection about when he actually came back, that document that's in front of you? It's still on the screen.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I wasn't the person who produced this document. It doesn't jog my memory, nor, indeed, do I believe that it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't know that the 30th personnel centre of the VJ is the place that's actually distributes the money, and that this document is to them so they know to stop giving you the that higher salary on a particular date? You disagree with that. You think this is a made-up document?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that it was fabricated or made-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what was wrong with General Djukic during that several month period, five months, roughly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Djukic was away, April, May, and June, up until mid-June or perhaps late June. I don't know exactly. I don't know the exact date he left, either, but it could not possibly have been more than three months altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's say it's three to four months -- or three months like you say. What was wrong with him?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he left to receive treatment, and he underwent surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Treatment for cancer?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Surgery for cancer can be extremely serious. How serious was the surgery?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say it was something that was easy. If it was an issue that serious, then it could hardly have been anything else but a difficult kind of surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, do you know that they actually remove organs and that kind of thing, or do they just, you know, do a biopsy. I don't expect that you would know the exact details of it, but I think that you would have a general idea?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, all I know is what I heard, and who knows if that is true or not. If the Court wants to happen exactly what I heard about that, well, I would be glad to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am asking you to tell us what you've heard about his condition, about the extent of his surgery. We probably all know people who have had this happen, so why don't you give us a bit an insight into it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I heard that he was off to get surgery for a pancreas cancer. I'm not sure if it was surgically removed in its entirely or not, and I'm not sure what type was surgery was performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. But he was not east never quite the same after he got back, was he? Especially in those first couple of weeks after he got back.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, upon his return, General Djukic, to much amazement for many a quarter [as interpreted] was perhaps not the old General Djukic but exercised the same -- exuded the same authority as ever before. So yes, he was the old General Djukic, you might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. When you were standing in for him, you had to know whole job not just your operations sector. You had to know the technical group and the other three or four units you've discussed, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, a truthful answer would be I should have known, but the worse part was that I could not have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 3954.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, if we could -- okay, I've handed you that. Now, this is from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. It's got a number 10/36 on it. What's the significance of that, before we get into the actual document?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm afraid I'm not sure what I'm expected to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, just take a look up in the left-hand corner, right under the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, it says: "Confidential number 10/36/4-132."

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this means that the document was produced at the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, the logistics sector, and the number is 10/36/4-132.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So if 10 is the logistics sector, what is the 36?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honours, I didn't say the 10 stood for logistics. I don't actually know what number was used for the logistics sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's the significance of number 36, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honours, I am unable to say. I am unable to say what 36 meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But if we just take a look at this, it says: "Standing in assistant commander more logistics." Is that you, on 27 May? And if it could come up so we can see the bottom, that was the ... Is that you or did somebody else in 27 May -- was someone else standing in for the assistant commander for logistics?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on 27th of May, 1995, I was the one standing in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you're the one that issued this order, as you see on the first page, it says: "I hereby order ..."

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That might be the inference, but I can't say that I was the one who dispatched this. Given the fact that the signature is missing, and on top of that I don't really remember this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I won't get into the whole document. Just the beginning we see that it has to do with fuel conservation and saving fuel. You don't remember being involved in ordering all these corps to do these particular measures?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, let's go to number 3955. And I'll hand you this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another document dated 27 May 1995, Main Staff of the army Republika Srpska. And NR, which means personally to Colonel Miljanovic, it talks about the request of storing supplies in the 35th logistics base in Bijeljina. And it's a request to do that. Somebody wants to store charged casings that are intended for the purchaser of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Do you remember facilitating this? This appears to be ammunition going to the federal republic in this situation.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 3943.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll give you a copy of that. This now is a 17 June 1995 document from the Main Staff, and your name is type-signed at the bottom of it, standing for the assistant commander, Colonel Ratko Miljanovic. And this sent, as we can see, to the logistic bases and many of the institutions I think that you listed for Ms. Fauveau when you were talking about the units of the logistic -- of your logistic sector. And it's really it looks like a -- it's called a greeting card on the occasion of St. Vitus day, and that's what it sounds like. It sounds like a moral-type greeting card: "On the contrary, the enemy like many times so far supported no not only by Islamic factor, but by NATO forces are making useless and desperate efforts to achieve their loathsome goals." Do you remember, did somebody write that for you or did you write that yourself?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I don't remember writing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you know nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the time being, based on what I see, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "For the time being," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there was a document showing my name there would be no doubt, would there. This being what it is, this is not my style. I don't write like this; therefore, I am unable to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, did you communicate with the logistics people, the people that are basically under your direction when you are standing in for General Djukic and communicate them about morale issues, propaganda issues, this sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as that is concerned, I never discussed that type of topic with anyone in my sector. That wasn't how I led my people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Were you involved in anything relating to supplying conscripts with supplies in around May or June of 1995 when you were standing in for General Djukic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I ask the interpreters just to repeat the beginning of the sentence. I didn't hear that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you involved in providing supplies equipping mobilized soldiers with supplies?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that at all. Well, I really cannot decidedly say whether I did or didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is, as you're reading it, another document out of the logistics sector of the Main Staff. This is 22 June. So we're now beyond mid-June. And it's the attention of several corps, including the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we go to the last page. Standing in for the assistant commander for logistics, Colonel Ratko Miljanovic, graduated engineer, with SR next to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is an order, again, it's entitled, "Equipping Mobilized Military Conscripts from the FRY." This is about personal weaponry. This is part of the every day work that the assistant commander for logistics is involved in, issuing orders, and in this case regarding the supply of conscripts. Is this you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it does state here my first and last name, but as to whether I wrote this or signed this, I have no recollection of that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this help refresh your recollection that you actually did get involved in equipping the troops? I mean, that's not a very radical thing for the assistant commander of logistics to be doing. It's certainly not a crime.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm what you are asserting. It's not the usual duty of the assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever, while you were standing in as assistant commander for logistics, ever do anything that's equipped any troops or assist in the equipping of any troops with any equipment, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about food, did you ever assist in providing the -- any of the troops with food? You know, helping the corps or the other units kind of facilitate food to the troops?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that question is directed at me, that I did that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, did you ever help facilitate the feeding of troops? Or help direct where they should be fed or who should feed them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. That was the job of the quarter master service. And this is the work that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, as assistant -- as standing in for the assistant commander of logistics, you had some supervision over the quarter master section, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the degree that I was able to do that objectively, physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not saying you're feeding him with a spoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me show you 3945.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another document out of the Main Staff logistics sector. And your name, standing in for the assistant commander for logistics, is to the command of the Drina Corps assistant commander for logistics, and command of the airforce and anti-aircraft Defence of the 1st Zvornik infantry brigade. And it's entitled "Feeding of man power and airforce and anti-aircraft defence." And it's entitled "Order." It references a telegram, and then says: "Airforce and anti-aircraft defence helicopter crews located for a longer time in Zvornik, 25 to 30 persons, should be fed at the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade." You ordered these crews to go eat at Vinko Pandurevic's brigade, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not ruling out that this is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're getting somewhere then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to another document, number 3957. Last one before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is again from the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, with that same number on it, 10/33. It's dated 14 July 1995, to the 27th POB and to the command of the Drina Corps, and pursuant to Article 175 of the law and a demonstrated need, it says, "I hereby order ..." And if we go to the end, it says, "Deputy assistant commander for rear service, Colonel Ratko Miljanovic." Now, you told us that sometimes when Djukic stepped out for a moment or something then you would sign off as his deputy, is this what -- is that what's going on here?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I signed as the deputy when he was physically not at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Where was Djukic on 14 July? You had a lot of time to think about these days before testifying.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that right now, Your Honours. I don't know where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how was it that this order -- where did you get the information to write up this order?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to draft this order, I was called by General Lukic [as interpreted] personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, General Djukic. They got the name wrong.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he tell you every bit of information in this or did you research and get some more information yourself?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Djukic practically dictated the entire contents as he was in the habit of doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, was there an officer named Kerkez at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was his full name?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Kerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Last question. What unit -- what branch or unit was he in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MILJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Zeljko Kerkez was the chief of the traffic section of the logistics section of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. It's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are stopping here today. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Same advisory as yesterday. Mr. Miljanovic, you are not to discuss with anyone the subject matter of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
